why: On your placement you got BOTH Vieta (Q5, +38s, "unsure of signs") and x±1/x (Q24, +51s) correct — but nearly a minute slow each because you were reconstructing the machinery live. The fix isn't more memorizing; it's owning the one expansion each pattern falls out of, so the signs and ladders become reflex instead of a nervous derivation at the buzzer.
overview: This bank leans on these two patterns hard, and they're pure speed plays — every question is a 5-second answer once the reflex is in. Vieta shows up as "sum/product/sum-of-reciprocals of roots" (2024-r4-b9), "build the monic polynomial from these roots" (2023-r4-b17), "find a coefficient given a root" (2024-r6-b11), and disguised as statistics ("std dev of the roots," 2024-r12-b4) or shifted roots ("subtract 2 from each root," 2024-r11-b6). The x±1/x family is always a power-ladder: given x+1/x, find (x−1/x)², x²+1/x², or x⁴+1/x⁴ (2025-r10-b7, 2023-r6-t11). Mindset: never re-derive signs at the buzzer — read them off the expansion of (x−r)(x−s)(x−t), and climb the ±1/x ladder by "square, subtract 2." Recognize the pattern in the first three words and the answer is arithmetic.

cards.title: Vieta signs come from ONE expansion — never memorize them
cards.body:
A monic cubic with roots r,s,t **is** (x−r)(x−s)(x−t). Expand and watch where each coefficient is born:

(x−r)(x−s)(x−t) = x³ − (r+s+t)x² + (rs+rt+st)x − rst

- **x² coeff**: pick one of −r,−s,−t → −(sum) → **sum = −b**
- **x coeff**: pick two roots at a time; two minus signs cancel → +(pairwise) → **pairwise = +c**
- **constant**: (−r)(−s)(−t) → −(product) → **product = −d**

The alternating sign is baked into the (−) inside each factor: every root you pick brings a minus, so an even number of picks is +, an odd number is −. You don't recall 'sum is minus, pairwise plus' — you SEE the sign flip with parity. If you ever blank, expand (x−r)(x−s) in one second and the pattern is obvious. This is the cure for 'unsure of signs.'

cards.title: Cubic x³+bx²+cx+d Vieta (monic)
cards.body:
sum = −b · pairwise (rs+rt+st) = +c · product (rst) = −d.
**Why:** they're the coefficients of (x−r)(x−s)(x−t) with signs set by parity (see the expansion card). General monic degree-n rule: coeff of x^{n−k} = (−1)ᵏ·(k-th elementary symmetric sum eₖ). Quadratic x²+bx+c: sum=−b, product=+c (k=1 flips, k=2 doesn't). **Non-monic?** Divide by the leading coeff first, or use sum=−(second)/(first), product=(−1)ⁿ·(last)/(first).

cards.title: Sum of reciprocals of roots = pairwise / product
cards.body:
Σ(1/r) = (rs+rt+st)/(rst) = e_{n−1}/eₙ. For a cubic x³+bx²+cx+d this is **c / (−d) = −c/d**.
**Why (two ways):** (1) Put 1/r+1/s+1/t over rst — the numerator is exactly the pairwise sum, no new formula. (2) *Faster mental model:* the reciprocals of the roots are the roots of the **coefficient-reversed** polynomial. Reverse x³+0x²+2x+1 → 1x³+2x²+0x+1, whose root-sum is −2/1 = **−2**. So 'sum of reciprocals' = 'sum of roots of the flipped poly' = −(2nd coeff)/(1st) after reversing. For x³+2x+1: −c/d = −2/1 = −2 (your Q5).

cards.title: The x±1/x ladder: the cross term is always ±2
cards.body:
Square anything of the form x±1/x and the middle term is 2·x·(1/x) = **±2**, always, because the x and 1/x annihilate:
(x+1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x²  →  x²+1/x² = (x+1/x)² − 2
(x−1/x)² = x² − 2 + 1/x²

Subtract the two identities: (x+1/x)² − (x−1/x)² = 4, so **(x−1/x)² = (x+1/x)² − 4**.

The whole ladder is 'square, subtract 2' because that cross term is pinned regardless of x. To climb: let pₙ = xⁿ+1/xⁿ. Then pₙ² = p_{2n} + 2 ⇒ **p_{2n} = pₙ² − 2**, so for x+1/x=3 you get 3→7→47 without ever finding x.

cards.title: x±1/x power ladder
cards.body:
Let s = x+1/x. Then:
- (x−1/x)² = **s² − 4**
- x² + 1/x² = **s² − 2**
- x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = **(s²−2)² − 2**
- x³ + 1/x³ = **s³ − 3s** (from s³ = x³+1/x³ + 3s)
Recurrences: (xⁿ+1/xⁿ)² = x²ⁿ+1/x²ⁿ + 2 (doubling), and pₙ·p₁ = p_{n+1} + p_{n−1} (stepping by one).
**Why:** every square deposits a fixed +2 cross term, so undo it by shaving 2. The cube identity is the same annihilation carried one term further.

cards.title: Words that fire each reflex
cards.body:
**'sum / product / sum of reciprocals of the roots'** → Vieta, read signs off coefficients (don't solve for roots!).
**'monic / leading coefficient 1 polynomial with roots ___'** → build (x−r)(x−s)(x−t); if a complex root a+bi is given with REAL coeffs, a−bi is forced; if a surd p+√q is given with RATIONAL/integer coeffs, p−√q is forced.
**'given x+1/x = k, find …'** → power ladder, square-and-subtract-2.
**'subtract/add k from each root, then multiply'** → shifted-root trick, evaluate f(k) or f(−k).
**'population standard deviation / mean / variance of the roots'** → Vieta feeds Var = (Σr²)/n − mean², with Σr² = (sum)²−2(pairwise).

cards.title: Fast path: 'population std dev of roots of x³−24x+5'
cards.body:
Vieta wearing a statistics hat. Roots r,s,t.
- mean = (r+s+t)/3 = (−b)/3 = 0/3 = **0** (no x² term ⇒ sum 0).
- Σr² = (sum)² − 2(pairwise) = 0² − 2(−24) = **48**.
- Var = Σr²/3 − mean² = 48/3 − 0 = 16 → std = **4**.
Three Vieta reads and a subtraction — no root-finding. Note 'population' means divide by n (=3); a 'sample' std would divide by n−1=2 and give a different number, so read that word. (2024-r12-b4, answer 4.)

cards.title: Shifted roots: product of (root − k) = (−1)ⁿ·f(k)
cards.body: If f(x) = (x−r)(x−s)(x−t), then f(k) = (k−r)(k−s)(k−t). So (r−k)(s−k)(t−k) = (−1)³·f(k) = −f(k) for a cubic — each of the n factors flips sign. **Just evaluate the polynomial at k; no roots needed.** For x³+4x+1, product of (root−2) = −f(2) = −(8+8+1) = −17 (2024-r11-b6). 'Add k to each root, then multiply' uses f(−k). Bonus: the *shifted polynomial itself* (roots all decreased by k) is f(x+k) — expand it if they ask for a coefficient of the shifted poly, not just the product.

cards.title: The traps that cost you 38–51 seconds
cards.body:
1) **Sign panic (your Q5).** You paused to recall 'is product minus or plus?' Kill it: the constant of (x−r)(x−s)(x−t) is (−r)(−s)(−t) = −rst, so product = −d for a cubic, +c for a quadratic (even # of roots ⇒ no flip). Read it, don't recall it.
2) **Solving for x on ±1/x problems (your Q24).** You do NOT need x. x+1/x=5 → (x−1/x)²=25−4=21 in one step. Chasing x=(5±√21)/2 is the 50-second trap.
3) **Wrong conjugate rule.** Complex root needs REAL coeffs to force a−bi; surd root p+√q needs RATIONAL/integer coeffs to force p−√q. Miss it and your degree is wrong.
4) **Sum of reciprocals ≠ 1/(product).** It's pairwise/product = −c/d. Classic distractor.
5) **Depressed cubic (no x² term) ⇒ sum of roots = 0** — free info, don't overlook it (that's what makes the std-dev problem trivial).

memorize.answer: −b (pairwise = +c, product = −d)
pairwise ÷ product = −c/d for a cubic (= sum of roots of the coefficient-reversed polynomial)
sum = −b, product = +c (even degree → product does NOT flip sign)
s² − 4
s² − 2 (climb ladder: square, subtract 2)
s³ − 3s
(−1)ⁿ · f(k) — just evaluate the polynomial at k

memorize.trigger: Real coeffs + root a+bi   |   rational coeffs + root p+√q
memorize.answer: conjugate a−bi (complex case) or p−√q (surd case) is also a root

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT Q5 (+38s, unsure of signs). Cubic x³+2x+1, sum of reciprocals of the (distinct) roots. Do NOT find the roots. The 'distinct' clause is a red herring — reassurance, not information.
practice.solution: Read off Vieta: c=2, d=1. Sum of reciprocals = pairwise/product = c/(−d) = −c/d = −2/1 = **−2**. Cross-check via the reverse-coefficient view: flip x³+0x²+2x+1 → x³+2x²+0x+1, whose root-sum is −2. One read, one division. Target under 5s.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT Q24 (+51s). x+1/x=5, find (x−1/x)². The 'positive real x' is a distractor — you never need x's value. Solving the quadratic is the 50-second trap you fell into.
practice.solution: (x−1/x)² = (x+1/x)² − 4 = 25 − 4 = **21**. The two squares differ only by twice the ±2 cross term (=4). Instant.

practice.note: Ladder-climb: x+1/x=3, find x⁴+1/x⁴. Two rungs of 'square, subtract 2.' Watch: don't stop at x²+1/x².
practice.solution: x²+1/x² = 3²−2 = 7. Then x⁴+1/x⁴ = 7²−2 = 49−2 = **47**. Each square adds a fixed +2 cross term, so subtract 2 each rung.

practice.note: Build monic cubic from roots. Given real root 2 and complex root 1+3i → real (here integer) coeffs force the conjugate 1−3i. Reverse-Vieta: compute the three symmetric sums, apply signs.
practice.solution: Roots {2, 1+3i, 1−3i}. Sum = 2+2 = 4 → x² coeff = −4. Pairwise = (1+3i)(1−3i) + 2·[(1+3i)+(1−3i)] = 10 + 2·2 = 14 → x coeff = +14. Product = 2·10 = 20 → constant = −20. Answer: **x³ − 4x² + 14x − 20**. (Speed tip: the conjugate pair collapses to the real quadratic x²−2x+10, then multiply by (x−2).)

practice.note: Shifted roots: x³+4x+1 with roots a,b,c; find (a−2)(b−2)(c−2). Textbook case for the f(k) trick — expanding the roots is the slow trap.
practice.solution: Product of (root − 2) = (−1)³·f(2) = −f(2). f(2) = 8 + 8 + 1 = 17. Answer = **−17**. (Because f(x)=∏(x−root) ⇒ f(2)=∏(2−root)=−∏(root−2).)

practice.note: Find a coefficient from a root: x³ + ax² + bx − 2 has root −1−√2, with a,b integers. Rational coeffs force the surd conjugate −1+√2. Fastest is to peel off the minimal polynomial of the surd pair.
practice.solution: The surd pair −1±√2 are roots of (x+1)²−2 = x²+2x−1. So f(x) = (x²+2x−1)(x−r₃), and the constant −1·(−r₃)=r₃ must equal −2 ⇒ r₃=−2. Then a = coeff of x² = 2 + (−r₃)… concretely f = (x²+2x−1)(x+2) = x³+4x²+3x−2, so **a = 4** (and b=3). Vieta cross-check: product of roots = −(−2)=2, conjugate pair multiplies to 1−2=−1, third root = 2/(−1)=−2, sum = −4 = −a ⇒ a=4.

practice.note: Population standard deviation of roots of x³−24x+5. Vieta in disguise — 'population' means divide variance by n=3, not n−1.
practice.solution: mean = −b/3 = 0 (no x² term). Σr² = (sum)²−2(pairwise) = 0−2(−24) = 48. Var = 48/3 − 0² = 16 ⇒ std = **4**. No cubic solving — three reads and a subtraction.

why: Your placement showed the exact three leaks this lesson targets: a correct-but-162s conditional (2025-r8-b4 — needs the cancel-the-denominators reflex), a WRONG tournament setup (2023-r12-b22 — you mis-handled the random pairing and forgot to average over the unknown final opponent), and a slow EV (2024-r6-t18 — brute-forced instead of using symmetry).
overview: Probability is one of the densest math categories in this bank, and the writers reuse four shapes relentlessly: "at least one / not a / all are drawn" (do the complement), "given …" (conditional — shrink the sample space), "expected value" (linearity/symmetry, essentially never the full distribution), and random pairings/tournaments (casework averaged over the unknown opponent). The fast mindset is to **name the shape in the first 2 seconds, then collapse to arithmetic** — flip to the complement, cancel the shared C(n,2) denominator, or write a count as a sum of 0/1 indicators. Almost every EV here dies to "total minus hidden" or "count x single probability," and almost every conditional here is "favorable-both / favorable-at-least-one" in raw counts. Understand *why* each shortcut is valid (below) so you can rederive it at the buzzer instead of misremembering a formula.

cards.title: The 4 probability shapes that actually appear here
cards.body:
This bank recycles four shapes. Name them instantly:

1. **"At least one" / "not a side" / "covered by at least one"** -> complement `1 - P(none)`. Ex: 2025-r5-t9 (decagon, not a side = 7/9), 2025-r13-b21 (subject covered = 10/3).
2. **"Given …"** -> conditional `P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B)`. Ex: 2025-r8-b4, 2025-r1-t8, 2025-r6-t1, 2024-r6-b6 (algebraic), plus Bayes: 2024-r9-b12, 2025-r16-t5.
3. **"Expected value / expected number"** -> linearity of expectation + indicators/symmetry; almost never build the distribution. Ex: 2024-r6-t18, 2025-r13-b21, 2024-r13-t12 (kings).
4. **Tournaments / random pairings** -> casework by who-plays-whom, then average over the unknown opponent. Ex: 2023-r12-b22, 2025-r15-t7.

Mindset: **do not compute the whole distribution.** Complement, condition, or use linearity to collapse to arithmetic.

cards.title: WHY "at least one" = 1 - P(none)
cards.body:
Every trial has exactly two outcomes for "success": zero successes, or one-or-more. These two buckets are complementary and cover the entire sample space, so their probabilities sum to 1. "At least one" is a fat, messy union (inclusion-exclusion hell); "none" is a single clean AND of independent failures. So `P(>=1) = 1 - P(all fail)`.

2025-r13-b21: 6 subjects, each of 2 players independently picks 2 of the 6. P(a given subject picked by nobody) = both players miss it = (2/3)(2/3) = 4/9, so P(covered) = 5/9. You never enumerate which subjects overlap.

Edge nuance: complement is only a shortcut when "none" is genuinely simpler. For "at least 5 of 7 heads" (2023-r6-t6) the complement P(<=4) has MORE terms than the direct tail C(7,5)+C(7,6)+C(7,7)=29 over 128 = 29/128 — so sum the SHORTER side, don't reflexively complement.

cards.title: WHY linearity of expectation is magic (works even when dependent!)
cards.body:
`E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y]` **always** — no independence needed — because expectation is a weighted average, and the average of a sum is the sum of averages (you may add each outcome's contributions in any order). This is the single biggest EV time-saver in the bank.

**Indicator trick:** to count "how many things happen," write count = sum of 0/1 indicators (one per thing), then `E[count] = sum of P(each thing happens)`. Overlaps between things do NOT break this — that is the whole point.
- 2025-r13-b21: E[covered subjects] = 6 x P(one subject covered) = 6(5/9) = **10/3**. (The subjects' coverages are dependent — linearity does not care.)
- 2024-r13-t12 (kings before first ace): E = 4 kings x P(a given king precedes all 4 aces) = 4 x 1/5 = **4/5** (among that 1 king + 4 aces, all 5 orders equally likely, so the king is first w.p. 1/5). No distribution — one probability times a count.

cards.title: Conditional probability — the exact reflex
cards.body:
`P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B)`. **Why:** conditioning on B throws away every outcome outside B and rescales what remains so it sums to 1; dividing by P(B) is that renormalization.

Two fast specializations:
- **"Given at least one X, prob both X"** = P(both X)/P(>=1 X), and since both live over the same C(n,2), work in **raw counts**: `C(fav,2) / [C(n,2) - C(non,2)]`. 2025-r8-b4 (4 red, 5 orange): 6 / (36 - 10) = 6/26 = **3/13**. The 36's cancel — never write them (this is your 162s leak).
- **"Rolls a die, sees an even number, EV?"** = conditioning deletes the odd outcomes, leaving {2,4,6} uniform -> mean = **4** (2025-r1-t8). The condition just erases the impossible outcomes; do not overthink it.

cards.title: EV shortcuts: total-minus-hidden, symmetric pairs, weighted
cards.body:
- **Hidden/visible via complement:** E[visible] = total - E[hidden], by linearity (E of a part removed subtracts). *Illustration* (not a bank ID): a die-corner's 3 hidden faces are the opposites of its 3 visible ones; sum of all 6 faces = 21, so E[3 visible] = 21 - E[3 hidden] = 21 - 21/2 = **21/2**.
- **Symmetric pairs:** if outcomes pair as {a, S-a}, one pick from a pair has expected value S/2. 2024-r6-t18: a corner touches 3 mutually adjacent faces = exactly one from each opposite pair {1,6},{2,5},{3,4}, each summing to 7 -> E = 3(7/2) = **21/2** (accept 10.5). Fastest of all.
- **Weighted, P proportional to f(i):** normalize, P(i) = f(i)/sum f. 2025-r5-t13 (P proportional to face value): P(1) = 1/(1+2+...+6) = **1/21**.

cards.title: Law of total probability & Bayes as an odds update
cards.body:
**Total probability:** `P(E) = sum over cases of P(E|case)P(case)` — split on a hidden cause, weight each branch. **Why:** the cases partition the sample space, so E's probability is its share within each branch, reweighted by how likely that branch is. 2025-r7-t5: 0.2(0.9) + 0.8(0.5) = **0.58**.

**Bayes, fast form:** posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio. **Why it's fast:** the common normalizing denominator P(data) cancels when you take the ratio of the two hypotheses, so you only compare likelihoods.
- 2024-r9-b12 (Timlandia, 2/3 truthful): P(3 of 4 say yes | snow):P(...| no snow) = (2/3)^3(1/3) : (1/3)^3(2/3) = 8:2 = 4:1, equal prior -> P(snow) = **4/5**.
- 2025-r16-t5 (Kokushi tiles): tampered has 3 haku vs untampered 4, so P(draw 3 haku | untampered):P(...| tampered) = C(4,3):C(3,3) = 4:1, equal prior -> P(tampered) = 1/(4+1) = **1/5**. Never drop the prior — the likelihood ratio alone is the answer only when the prior is 1:1.

cards.title: Word -> weapon (decide in 2 seconds)
cards.body:
- "**at least one**", "**not a**", "**covered/specialized by at least one**" -> complement `1 - P(none)` — but if it's "**at least k of n**", sum whichever tail has FEWER terms (do not blind-complement).
- "**Given**", "**knowing that**", "**sees a/an**" -> conditional; shrink the sample space, divide by P(condition), keep raw counts.
- "**expected**", "**on average**", "**expected number of**" -> linearity/indicators; hunt for symmetry or total-minus-hidden before any distribution.
- "**randomly paired**", "**bracket**", "**seeding is random**", "**tournament**" -> casework on matchups, average over the unknown opponent.
- "**proportional to**" -> normalize by the sum.
- "**wins the series in game 7**" -> tied 3-3 after 6 (C(6,3)/2^6 with a fair coin), then win game 7. General "**in game N**" = exactly 3 wins in first N-1 games, then win game N.
- "**before he draws the … / first ace**" -> symmetry/uniform relative order, not a geometric grind.

cards.title: WORKED: the tournament you missed (2023-r12-b22 -> 7/27)
cards.body:
4 players randomly paired -> 3 equally likely pairings, so **Alice's round-1 opponent is uniform over {B,C,D}, prob 1/3 each.** Template: `P(Alice champ) = sum_opp (1/3) P(beat opp) P(win final)`, and **P(win final) MUST average over whoever survives the other bracket** — this is the step you dropped.

- **Opp = B (1/3):** beat B w.p. 1/3; other bracket is C vs D, and Alice beats either w.p. 2/3, so P(final win) = 2/3. Contribution: (1/3)(1/3)(2/3) = **2/27**.
- **Opp = C (1/3):** beat C w.p. 2/3; other bracket B vs D -> final foe is B (w.p. 3/4, Alice wins 1/3) or D (w.p. 1/4, Alice wins 2/3). P(final win) = (3/4)(1/3)+(1/4)(2/3) = 1/4+1/6 = **5/12**. Contribution: (1/3)(2/3)(5/12) = **5/54**.
- **Opp = D (1/3):** symmetric to C -> **5/54**.

Total = 2/27 + 5/54 + 5/54 = 4/54 + 5/54 + 5/54 = 14/54 = **7/27**.

cards.title: WORKED: corner-of-die EV in 5 seconds (2024-r6-t18 -> 21/2)
cards.body: Slow way (your placement path): list all 8 corners, sum each triple, divide by 8. Fast way: a corner's three faces are mutually adjacent, hence **one face from each of the three opposite pairs** {1,6},{2,5},{3,4}. Each pair sums to 7, and by symmetry a random corner is equally likely to take either member, so expected pick per pair = 7/2. Three independent pairs -> 3(7/2) = **21/2** (accept 10.5). No enumeration. (Cross-check: total over all 8 corners = each face touches 4 corners = 4(21) = 84, /8 = 10.5.)

cards.title: Your three leaks — patch these
cards.body:
1. **Conditional CORRECT but 162s (2025-r8-b4).** You computed P(both) and P(>=1) as full fractions then divided. Skip it: raw counts, `C(4,2)/[C(9,2)-C(5,2)] = 6/26 = 3/13`. The C(9,2)=36 cancels — never write it. Target < 20s.
2. **Tournament WRONG (2023-r12-b22): mis-set-up the pairing.** Two classic errors: (a) forgetting the final opponent is random and must be averaged (not assumed), (b) mishandling that Alice's own R1 opponent is uniform 1/3. Always write `sum_opp (1/3) P(beat)[sum_finalfoe P(advance) P(beat)]`.
3. **EV slow (2024-r6-t18): brute-forced.** Reflex for ANY EV: can I write it as total - hidden, a sum of indicators, or a symmetric pairing — before touching a distribution?

**Distractor watch:** 2023-r3-t11 "smallest number rolled is 5" is NOT "both >= 5" — it's exactly-min-5, so from the 4 outcomes in {5,6}x{5,6} subtract (6,6): 3/36 = **1/12**.

memorize.answer: 1 - P(none); P(none) = product of independent failures. Never do inclusion-exclusion. Exception: 'at least k of n' — sum the shorter tail directly.

memorize.trigger: 'Given at least one is red, prob both red'
memorize.answer: P(both)/P(>=1) = C(fav,2) / [C(n,2) - C(non,2)]; denominators cancel, work in raw counts. Balls(4,5): 6/26 = 3/13.
P(A and B)/P(B). Conditioning deletes outcomes outside B and renormalizes by dividing by P(B).
= E[X]+E[Y], ALWAYS, no independence needed. To count things, sum indicators: E[count] = sum P(each happens), even with overlaps.
Total - E[hidden], or symmetric pairs. Die corner = one face from each opposite pair {1,6}{2,5}{3,4}: 3 x 7/2 = 21/2.

memorize.trigger: 4 players randomly paired into a bracket
memorize.answer: 3 equally likely pairings; your R1 opponent uniform 1/3 over the others; then AVERAGE the final over who advances from the other side.
P(i) = f(i)/sum f(i). P proportional to face value on a 6-die: P(1) = 1/21.
posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio; common denominator cancels. Timlandia 3/4-say-yes -> 4:1 -> 4/5. Never drop the prior.
Tied 3-3 after 6 games, then win game 7. Fair coin: C(6,3)/2^6 x 1/2 = (20/64)(1/2) = 5/32.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT Q2 — right but 162s. Goal: under 20s. The whole point is to NOT write the C(9,2) denominators.
practice.solution: 'Given >=1 red, both red' = P(both red)/P(>=1 red). Work in raw counts over C(9,2)=36: both red = C(4,2)=6; no red = C(5,2)=10, so >=1 red = 36-10=26. Answer = 6/26 = **3/13**. The 36 cancels — never write it.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT Q9 — WRONG (mis-set-up the pairing). This is THE template tournament problem; drill the setup until automatic.
practice.solution: Alice's R1 opponent is uniform 1/3 over {B,C,D}. Opp=B: (1/3)(beat B=1/3)(final vs C or D, win=2/3)=2/27. Opp=C: (1/3)(2/3)(final: B w.p.3/4 -> win 1/3, D w.p.1/4 -> win 2/3 => 5/12)=5/54. Opp=D: symmetric=5/54. Sum = 2/27+5/54+5/54 = 14/54 = **7/27**.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT Q20 — EV, slow. Kill the enumeration with opposite-pairs symmetry.
practice.solution: A corner touches 3 mutually adjacent faces = one from each opposite pair {1,6},{2,5},{3,4}. Each pair sums to 7; expected member = 7/2. Three pairs: 3(7/2) = **21/2** (accept 10.5).

practice.note: 'At least one' + linearity combo — the pattern for EV of a count with overlaps. Linearity ignores the overlaps.

Reinforces YOUR tournament leak: casework on random seeding, higher skill always wins. Correct answer 2/3.

why: On placement you missed BOTH easy stats questions from one root cause: variance lives in squared units. Q17 (2023-r6-b18) you scaled variance by 3 instead of 3²=9 (answer 162), and Q3 (2025-r11-t15) you didn't have the Poisson = "count in an interval" phrasing reflex. Both are 2-second buzzes once the "why" clicks.
overview: Bank stats splits cleanly into two buckets. **Distribution questions are pure sight-ID** — match phrasing to Poisson/exponential/binomial/geometric/normal (plus the trivia pair: multinomial = "generalized binomial," Cauchy = ratio of two normals / undefined mean). Win these in 2 seconds by reading for the trigger word, not by reasoning. **Computation questions** hammer three tools relentlessly: variance scales by k² (SD by |k|), variances ADD for sums *and* differences, and Var = RMS² − mean². Every one of those three is really the same fact — variance is an average of *squared* deviations, so it lives in squared units. Internalize that single idea and the whole computation half becomes reflex.

cards.title: The 5-distribution sight-ID table
cards.body:
Nearly every distribution tossup is a pure ID. Match the *phrasing*, not the math:

| Words in the question | Distribution |
|---|---|
| **count** of events in a **fixed interval** (per second / per area / per page) | **Poisson** |
| **time until / between** events, until failure/burnout | **Exponential** |
| # successes in a **fixed number n** of trials | **Binomial** |
| # trials **until the first** success | **Geometric** |
| a **measured** continuous quantity (heights, lengths, errors) | **Normal** |

Mnemonic: *Count in a window → Poisson; wait on the clock → Exponential; fixed tries → Binomial; tries till first → Geometric; a measurement → Normal.*

Speed cue: the two lures Science Bowl always plants next to a Poisson answer are **time**-based ("time between," "time until") — those are Exponential. If the stem says *count/number of*, it's Poisson; if it says *time/how long*, it's Exponential.

cards.title: Why variance scales by k² and SD by |k| (your Q17 miss)
cards.body:
Variance is the **average of *squared* deviations** from the mean. Multiply every data point by k → every deviation from the mean is also ×k → every *squared* deviation is **×k²**. Averaging k²-times-bigger squared deviations gives a variance that's k² times bigger.

SD = √variance = √(k²·Var) = **|k|·SD**. The absolute value is because √(k²)=|k|, so k=−3 scales SD by 3, not −3.

So Var(3X) = 3²·18 = **162**, not 3·18 = 54. That's the whole Q17 trap: you scaled variance by 3, but variance is in *squared units* — it must scale by the *square* of the multiplier.

cards.title: Why variances ADD — even for a difference
cards.body:
For independent X, Y: **Var(X±Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y)**. Expand E[((X−μ_X)±(Y−μ_Y))²]: the cross-term is ±2·Cov(X,Y), which is 0 for independent variables, so only the two squared spreads survive — and they add.

The killer case: **Var(X−Y) also = Var(X)+Var(Y)**. Write X−Y = X+(−1)Y; by the k² rule Var(−Y)=(−1)²Var(Y)=Var(Y). The minus sign gets *squared away*. Intuition: subtracting an independent noisy quantity makes the result *more* uncertain, not less — spreads never cancel.

Heights of men minus women: Var = 3+4 = 7, SD = **√7**. Never subtract variances. The planted distractor is √(4−3)=1.

cards.title: Binomial mean & SD (+ the fair-coin shortcut)
cards.body:
Binomial(n, p): **mean = np**, **Var = np(1−p)**, **SD = √(np(1−p))**.

**Why:** one Bernoulli trial X∈{0,1} has X²=X, so Var = E[X²]−E[X]² = p−p² = p(1−p). n independent trials → variances add → np(1−p). (Mean is np because each trial contributes p on average.)

**Fair-coin shortcut:** p=½ ⇒ np(1−p)=n/4 ⇒ **SD = √n / 2**. Ten thousand fair coins: √10000/2 = 100/2 = **50** (mean 5000). Recognizing "fair coins" lets you skip plugging into np(1−p) entirely — just √n over 2.

cards.title: Var = E[X²] − (mean)² = RMS² − mean²
cards.body:
**Var = E[X²] − (E[X])².** Since RMS = √(E[X²]), this reads **Var = RMS² − mean²**.

**Why:** expand E[(X−μ)²] = E[X²] − 2μE[X] + μ² = E[X²] − μ² (since E[X]=μ). It's literally *mean-of-squares minus square-of-mean* — and it's always ≥ 0, which is exactly why RMS ≥ mean.

Gas cloud: RMS=60, mean=50 ⇒ Var = 3600−2500 = 1100 ⇒ SD = √1100 ≈ **33**. Speed cue: whenever a stem hands you *both* an RMS/quadratic-mean and an arithmetic mean and asks for SD or spread, it's this identity — subtract the squares, take the root.

cards.title: Transformations: what X → aX + b does to every statistic
cards.body:
Under X → aX + b:

- **Mean, median, mode → a·(stat) + b** — all three centers shift by b and scale by a (a>0 preserves order, so median/mode ride along)
- **Variance → a²·Var** (the b vanishes — a rigid shift moves data without spreading it)
- **SD → |a|·SD**, **Range → |a|·Range**, **IQR → |a|·IQR**

One idea covers it: **adding a constant never touches spread; only multiplying does.** Centers move with b; spreads ignore b entirely. This is the same k² fact wearing a different hat — spread measures scale by |a| (SD, range, IQR) or a² (variance), never by b.

cards.title: Skew: mean vs median, and outlier robustness
cards.body:
**Right-skewed (long right tail) ⇒ mean > median** — the tail drags the mean toward it. The clean textbook examples are **geometric and exponential** (both strictly mean > median). **Symmetric ⇒ mean = median:** normal, uniform, binomial at p=½.

A subtlety worth knowing: **Poisson is positively skewed but its mean ≈ median** — for integer λ they're actually *equal* (λ=1,2,3,5,10 all give median = mean = λ), so Poisson is a bad illustration of "mean > median." Use geometric/exponential for that claim.

Watch the other edge case: **binomial is symmetric ONLY at p=½** (skewed left if p>½, right if p<½). In a "which has mean > median?" list like {uniform, normal, binomial, geometric}, the intended symmetric-binomial reading makes **geometric** the unique answer.

**Outlier robustness:** median and mode barely move; mean, range, variance, SD blow up. Multiply one score by 1000 → the **median** changes least (it only cares about *rank*, not magnitude).

cards.title: Instant word-triggers
cards.body:
- 'number of ___ in [1 second / per unit area / per page]' → **Poisson**
- 'time between' / 'until it burns out' / 'until the next' → **Exponential**
- 'measured lengths/heights/errors' → **Normal**
- 'trials until the first success' → **Geometric**; 'successes in n trials' → **Binomial**
- 'multiplied by k, new variance?' → **×k²** (SD ×|k|, range ×|k|)
- 'variance/SD of a sum OR a difference' → **ADD the variances**
- 'RMS ___ and mean ___, find SD' → **√(RMS² − mean²)**
- 'accidentally ×10 / ×1000 one value, which stat changes least?' → **median**
- 'generalized binomial' → **Multinomial**; 'ratio of two normals / has no mean / undefined mean' → **Cauchy**
- 'memoryless' → **Exponential** (continuous) or **Geometric** (discrete)

cards.title: The four traps that cost you points
cards.body:
1. **Variance scaling (your Q17):** ×k on data → ×**k²** on variance, never ×k. Only SD/range scale by |k|. 18→162, not 54.
2. **Poisson vs Exponential (your Q3):** *count* in an interval = Poisson; *time* between/until = Exponential. The stem surrounds the one Poisson answer with time-based lures ('time between trains,' 'time until burnout') — pick the *count*.
3. **Difference of variances:** you still **ADD** (√7, not √1). The minus sign gets squared.
4. **Adding a constant:** shifts mean/median/mode by b but leaves variance/SD/range/IQR *untouched* — don't scale spread at all for a pure shift.

Eliminate: measured ruler lengths = Normal; time a lightbulb lasts = Exponential; time between trains = Exponential. The pattern is one 'count in a window' answer surrounded by two 'time' distractors plus a 'measurement' distractor — read for *number of* vs *time*, and pick the count.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT MISS (Q17). Variance scales by the SQUARE of the multiplier. You used ×3 (→54); correct is ×3²=×9.
practice.solution: Multiply every element by 3 → variance ×3² = ×9. 18×9 = **162 (Z)**. Why: variance averages *squared* deviations, so each deviation ×3 makes each squared deviation ×9. (SD would scale by only 3; the ×3 answer, 54, is the planted trap you fell for.)

practice.note: Binomial SD. Recognize n=10000 Bernoulli(½) and use the fair-coin shortcut — don't bother computing the mean.
practice.solution: SD = √(np(1−p)) = √(10000·½·½) = √2500 = **50 (X)**. Fast path: fair coin ⇒ SD = √n/2 = √10000/2 = 100/2 = 50. (Distractor 500 = the mean-ish scale trap; 100 = √n without the /2.)

practice.note: Variance of a DIFFERENCE of independent normals. The trap is subtracting variances.
practice.solution: For independent variables, Var of the difference = SUM of variances (the −1 gets squared): 3 + 4 = 7. SD = **√7** (the bank stores '7' under the radical). Never do √(4−3)=1 — subtracting an independent quantity adds uncertainty, it doesn't cancel it.

practice.note: Skew ID. Among uniform/normal/binomial/geometric, find the one with mean > median (right-skewed).
practice.solution: Geometric is right-skewed (long right tail of large trial-counts), so its mean is pulled above its median → **Geometric (Z)**. Uniform and normal are symmetric; binomial is symmetric at the intended p=½ — all three give mean = median.

practice.note: The Var = E[X²]−(E[X])² identity in disguise: RMS and mean given, find SD. Two sig figs.
practice.solution: Var = RMS² − mean² = 60² − 50² = 3600 − 2500 = 1100. SD = √1100 ≈ 33.2 → **33**. This is exactly Var = E[X²]−(E[X])² because RMS² = E[X²] and mean² = (E[X])². Trigger: both an RMS and an arithmetic mean in one stem → subtract the squares, take the root.

topic: Fast Geometry: triples, centers, area shortcuts
why: On the placement you got the space-diagonal problem right but bled 78 seconds because you subtracted 169−9−144 instead of recognizing the 3-4-12-13 quad on sight, and you lost the incenter tossup outright ("idk what an incenter is"). Both are pure pattern-recall gaps — exactly the buzzer speed this lesson closes, while extending the hexagon decomposition you already nailed in 8s.
overview: This bank's geometry tossups reward recognition, not derivation. The writers recycle a tiny set of objects: Pythagorean triples/quads hidden inside prisms, rhombi, and right triangles (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 6-8-10, 3-4-12-13); the three triangle centers (incenter shows up most, then circumcenter); and area-by-decomposition on regular polygons. The fast mindset: **before you write anything, ask "what triple/shape is this?"** A box with edges 3, 12 and diagonal 13 should fire "3-4-12-13 → missing edge 4" in under 3 seconds, not trigger a 169−9−144 subtraction. Nearly every geometry answer in this bank is an integer or a clean radical, which is itself a signal you're meant to *see* a triple, not grind.

cards.title: The triples & quads to know cold
cards.body:
**2D triples:** 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29, 9-40-41 — plus every scaling (6-8-10, 9-12-15, 10-24-26...).

**3D quads (a²+b²+c²=d²):** **3-4-12-13** (the one that cost you 78s), **6-8-24-26** (=2×3-4-12-13, and it appears in this bank), 1-2-2-3, 2-3-6-7, 4-4-7-9.

*Why the quad works — this IS the trick:* a space diagonal is Pythagoras done twice. Face diagonal = √(a²+b²); then up to the far corner, diagonal = √(facediag²+c²) = √(a²+b²+c²). So you can chain two triples through a shared leg: (3,4,**5**) gives 3²+4²=5²; then (**5**,12,13) gives 5²+12²=13². Substitute: 3²+4²+12² = 5²+12² = 13². A quad is literally two triples welded at a 5.

cards.title: Why r = Area/s (and Area/perimeter = r/2)
cards.body:
Draw segments from the incenter I to all three vertices, slicing the triangle into 3 small triangles with bases a, b, c. The incenter is *equidistant from all three sides* — that distance is the inradius r — so each small triangle has height exactly r.

Area = ½r·a + ½r·b + ½r·c = r·(a+b+c)/2 = **r·s** (s = semiperimeter).

So r = Area/s, and Area/perimeter = rs/(2s) = **r/2**. Rebuild both from that one picture if you blank. (Note s = semiperimeter = perimeter/2 — the ½ is where the r/2 comes from.)

cards.title: Why AI = r / sin(A/2) — and a √ cross-check
cards.body:
I sits on the bisector of angle A, so AI splits angle A into two halves of A/2. Drop the perpendicular from I to side AB; its length is r (I is r from every side). That makes a right triangle: hypotenuse AI, the r-leg *opposite* the A/2 angle at A. So sin(A/2) = r/AI → **AI = r / sin(A/2)**. Same logic gives BI, CI with B/2, C/2.

*Cross-check with no trig:* the tangent length from A to the incircle is s−a (a = side opposite A). The r-leg and that tangent leg form a right triangle with hypotenuse AI, so **AI = √(r² + (s−a)²)**. Both routes must agree — a fast way to self-verify at the buzzer.

cards.title: Circumradius reflexes
cards.body:
**Right triangle: R = hypotenuse / 2.** *Why:* the circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse (Thales — the right angle subtends the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is a diameter). So R=5 ⇒ hyp=10; if a leg is 6, the other is 8 (6-8-10) ⇒ area = ½·6·8 = 24.

**Any triangle: R = abc / (4·Area).** *Why:* law of sines gives a = 2R·sin A, and Area = ½bc·sin A ⇒ sin A = 2·Area/(bc); substitute to get R = abc/(4·Area). Rarely needed here — know it exists for the odd bonus. (Sanity: 3-4-5 ⇒ 60/(4·6)=2.5 = hyp/2 ✓.)

cards.title: Area shortcuts that show up here
cards.body:
• **Equilateral:** (√3/4)·s². *Why:* the altitude cuts it into a 30-60-90 with hypotenuse s, so height = (√3/2)s; area = ½·s·height.
• **Regular hexagon:** 6 equilateral triangles = (3√3/2)s². Apothem = (√3/2)s, circumradius = s, so **apothem:radius = √3/2**.
• **Rhombus / kite:** ½·d₁·d₂. *Why:* perpendicular diagonals cut it into 4 right triangles with legs d₁/2, d₂/2.
• **Two sides + included angle:** ½·a·b·sin C (the b·sinC is just the height onto side a).
• **Trapezoid:** ½(b₁+b₂)·h (average base × height).
• **Heron memorized outputs:** 13-14-15 → **84**, 5-12-13 → 30, 9-12-15 → 54.

cards.title: Words that fire each technique
cards.body:
• "rectangular prism / box / space diagonal" → quad. Do 3-4-12-13 and 6-8-24-26 on sight; else √(a²+b²+c²).
• "incenter / inradius / incircle" → r = Area/s; AI = r/sin(A/2) = √(r²+(s−a)²); Area/perimeter = r/2.
• "circumradius / circumcenter" + right triangle → R = hyp/2.
• "regular hexagon/pentagon, area" → decompose into equilateral triangles / triangles-from-center.
• "rhombus" + "diagonals ... integer" → ½d₁d₂; halves satisfy p²+q²=side² (hunt a triple).
• side lengths 6-8-10, 5-12-13, 13-14-15 quoted → disguised triple; find the right angle or use area 24/30/84.

cards.title: Worked at buzzer speed: incenter AI (your missed Q)
cards.body:
*ABC: AB=6, BC=10, CA=8, inradius 2, find AI.*

1. 6-8-10 = 2×(3-4-5) → **right angle at A** (legs AB=6, CA=8 meet at A; BC=10 is the hypotenuse opposite A). ~2s.
2. AI = r/sin(A/2) = 2/sin45° = 2/(√2/2) = 4/√2 = **2√2**. ~3s.

*Where the trap answer 8 comes from:* AI² = r² + (s−a)² = 2² + 2² = 8. Someone who builds that right triangle but forgets the square root writes **8** — exactly the answer the bank says DO NOT ACCEPT. Anchor to "AI, not AI²" and you sidestep it. (s = 12, s−a = 12−10 = 2.)

cards.title: The four traps in this bank
cards.body:
1. **Grinding instead of recognizing** — your 78s space diagonal. Train the triple to fire *before* the pencil moves.
2. **Not knowing the center** — your incenter miss. Incenter = angle-bisector meet = incircle center, equidistant from the three *sides*. Circumcenter = perpendicular-bisector meet, equidistant from the three *vertices*. Don't swap them.
3. **Half-diagonal vs full diagonal** in rhombi: p²+q²=side² gives *half*-diagonals; area uses the *full* ones. Side 5 → halves 3,4 → fulls 6,8 → area 24, not 6. (Edge case: a rhombus of side s maxes out at area s² when it's a square — that's why 'side 13, area 170' is impossible, 170 > 169.)
4. **Forgetting the √ (or the /2)**: AI = √(r²+(s−a)²) not AI²=8; A/2 not A in AI=r/sin(A/2); s = perimeter/2 in r=Area/s.

why: On Q8 (2024-r2-t13) you wrote "3+x=27+8" — you shoved the log symbols around like ordinary numbers instead of asking "base to what power?" The single habit "a log IS an exponent" turns that whole problem into two five-second steps and kills the entire class of errors.
overview: Science Bowl logs are never calculus — they test one reflex: **a logarithm is the exponent you would write on the base.** The bank hammers five sub-patterns, all seen in real tossups: (1) evaluate a clean log by rewriting as an exponent (`log_27 3`, your placement miss); (2) collapse a `10^(log...)` / `b^(log_b x)` cancellation — often with a deliberate base mismatch; (3) break one big log using the power + product rules and the values of log2, log3 they hand you; (4) combine two same-base logs into one, then convert to an exponent equation; (5) recognize a power law `y=x^n` as a straight LINE of slope n on a log-log plot. The fast mindset: **never push log symbols around algebraically — turn each log into "base to what power = argument?" and it becomes arithmetic.** Almost every answer is a small integer or a simple fraction; an ugly result means you mis-set-up or flipped a ratio.

cards.title: A log IS an exponent (the whole topic in one line)
cards.body:
`log_b(a) = c` means exactly `b^c = a`. Read it aloud as **"b to the WHAT gives a?"** — the log's *value* is that exponent.

Read these instantly:
- `log_2 8` → 2 to the what = 8 → **3**
- `log_27 3` → 27 to the what = 3 → **1/3** (cube root, since 27=3³)
- `log_10 1000` → **3**; `log_5 1` → **0**; `log_7 7` → **1**

Speed cue: if the argument is **smaller than the base**, the answer is a proper fraction (0<c<1); if the argument is 1, the answer is 0; if base = argument, it's 1. This is the exact fix for your placement miss — you never *manipulate* the log letters, you *ask the question* and read off a number.

cards.title: WHY the product & power rules hold (it's just exponents adding)
cards.body:
Write the numbers as powers of the base: `x=b^m`, `y=b^n`. Since `b^m·b^n=b^(m+n)`, multiplying **adds** exponents — and a log *is* the exponent. So:
- `log(xy)=log x+log y` (multiply → add)
- `log(x/y)=log x−log y` (divide → subtract)
- `log(x^k)=k·log x` (`x^k` is x multiplied k times, so its exponent is added k times)

You are not memorizing three rules — they are one fact (exponents add under multiplication) viewed through the log. Under pressure, reconstruct any of them by writing `x=b^m` and reading off the exponent. Corollary you'll use: **a sum of logs of many numbers is the log of their product**, e.g. `log1+log2+…+log7 = log(7!)`.

cards.title: WHY b^(log_b x)=x, and where change-of-base comes from
cards.body:
**Cancellation:** `b^(log_b x)` says "raise b to the exponent that turns b into x." Applying that exponent to b gives x *by definition* — so `b^(log_b x)=x` and `log_b(b^x)=x`. They are inverse operations, like squaring a square root.

**Change of base:** to get `log_b a`, set `a=b^c`. Take log-base-anything of both sides: `log a = c·log b`, so `c = log a/log b`. Hence `log_b a = ln a/ln b = log₁₀a/log₁₀b`. Swapping a,b inverts it: `log_b a = 1/log_a b`.

**Fast corollary for the cancel trap:** `a^(log_{a^k} N) = N^(1/k)`. (Proof: `log_{a^k}N = (log_a N)/k`, so `a^{(log_a N)/k} = (a^{log_a N})^{1/k} = N^{1/k}`.) That's why `10^(log_100 49) = 49^{1/2} = 7` in one glance.

cards.title: The six things to have cold (with the WHY on each)
cards.body:
1. `log_b(a)=c ⇔ b^c=a` — *the definition; everything below is a consequence.*
2. `log(xy)=log x+log y`, `log(x/y)=log x−log y` — *multiplying = adding exponents.*
3. `log(x^k)=k·log x` — *k copies of the exponent added.*
4. `b^(log_b x)=x`, `log_b(b^x)=x` — *inverse ops cancel (only when bases match).* 
5. `log_b a = (log a)/(log b) = 1/(log_a b)` — *set a=b^c, take log of both sides.*
6. `a^(log_{a^k} N)=N^(1/k)` — *base-mismatch cancel: the outer/inner base ratio becomes the root.*

Carry two numbers: `log₁₀2≈0.301`, `log₁₀3≈0.477`. Derive the rest live: `log4=2·0.301=0.602`, `log5=1−log2=0.699`, `log6=log2+log3=0.778`, `log8=3·0.301=0.903`, `log9=2·0.477=0.954`.

cards.title: The exact words → the move
cards.body:
- **"log base x of …", or a lone log to evaluate** → rewrite as `base^(?) = arg`; answer the exponent.
- **"ten raised to the power of log base …" / any `b^(log …)`** → cancel to the argument; if bases differ use `a^(log_{a^k}N)=N^(1/k)`.
- **"base ten logarithm of 2 is 0.301 … logarithm of 6^1000"** → power rule pulls the exponent out front, product rule splits the base into the primes they gave you.
- **Two same-base logs added/subtracted ("log₁₂(x+y)+log₁₂(x−y)=2")** → combine into ONE log, then `arg = base^(RHS)`.
- **"sum of the base-ten logarithm of each of the first n integers"** → it's `log(n!)`; estimate the factorial's size.
- **"on a log-log scale" + a power like 1/x², x³** → straight LINE; **slope = the exponent** (its sign included). Never "parabola/exponential curve."
- **"squares the number every day" / "natural log every day"** → value is `3^(2^n)`; ln pulls the top exponent down → it **doubles** daily.

cards.title: Your placement question, in 5 seconds
cards.body:
`log_x 8 = log_27 3`.

**Step 1 — evaluate the RHS to a number first:** `log_27 3` = "27 to the what = 3?" 27=3³, so it's **1/3**.

**Step 2 — now `log_x 8 = 1/3`:** "x to the 1/3 = 8" means ∛x = 8, so `x = 8³ = 512`.

The trap you hit (`3+x=27+8`) came from reading it as an algebra equation in the *symbols*. It isn't — the right side collapses to one number, then the left side is one exponent equation. Two questions, two numbers, done.

cards.title: Cancellation with a deliberate base mismatch: 10^(log_100 49)
cards.body:
`10^(log_100 49)` (2023-r3-t15). Bases differ (10 vs 100), so it does **not** cancel directly — the test is checking whether you notice.

**Fast path:** 100 = 10², so use `a^(log_{a^k}N)=N^(1/k)` with a=10, k=2: answer `= 49^(1/2) = **7**`. 

**Long path (same result):** `log_100 49 = (log 49)/(log 100) = (log 49)/2 = log(49^{1/2}) = log 7`, then `10^(log 7)=7`.

Distractor map: **W) 1/7** = you flipped the exponent's sign (49^(−1/2)); **X) 1/2** = you stopped at the root exponent and forgot to apply it to 49; **Y) 2** = grabbed the "2" from 10². The lesson: cancellation needs outer base = inner-log base; convert until they match.

cards.title: The traps (including the one that cost you Q8) and their canned distractors
cards.body:
1. **Logs as algebra symbols** — your `3+x=27+8`. A log is a *question with a numeric answer*: evaluate it, don't shuffle it.
2. **Assuming `b^(log_c x)=x` when b≠c** — only cancels with matching bases (the 10-vs-100 trap; distractors 1/7, 1/2, 2).
3. **`log(x+y) ≠ log x + log y`.** The sum rule is for `log(xy)`. So `log₁₂(x+y)+log₁₂(x−y)=log₁₂((x+y)(x−y))=log₁₂(x²−y²)` — the classic buster.
4. **Sign/subtract slip when de-logging:** after `x²−y²=144` with y=5 you *add*: x²=169, x=13. The bait answer **119 = 144−25** is there for people who subtract.
5. **Fractional exponents:** `27^(1/3)=∛27=3`, not 27/3; `log_27 3=1/3`. Argument < base ⇒ fraction < 1. A huge answer means you flipped the ratio.
6. **log-log slope, with sign:** `y=1/x²=x^(−2)` ⇒ `log y=−2 log x` ⇒ a LINE of slope **−2**. Never pick "parabola" or "exponential decay curve" — those describe the *linear-axis* look.

overview: This bank hammers three reflexes: **CRT** ("remainder r1 when divided by n1, r2 by n2..., find the minimum"), **Legendre / trailing-zeros** ("exponent of prime p in N!", "how many zeroes at the end of N! in base b"), and **totient / roots of unity** ("how many primitive nth roots", "largest totient", "which cannot be a totient"). Every one is a plug-in formula, not a search — winners compute one expression instead of enumerating. Your mindset: the instant you hear the trigger words, fire the formula and read the answer off. Two specific speedups the writers reward: for CRT, check whether every remainder falls short of its divisor by the *same* amount d (then x = lcm - d, a one-line answer); for anything "N! in base b", it is just Legendre's floor-sum, then divide by the base's exponent.

cards.title: The three trigger phrasings — hear these, fire the formula
cards.body:
**"remainder r1 divided by n1, r2 by n2..., minimum x"** (or story-dressed: "rows of 4, 2 left over; rows of 5, 3 left over...") -> **CRT**.

**"exponent of p in N!" / "zeroes at the end of N! in base b" / "largest power of k dividing N!"** -> **Legendre floor-sum**.

**"how many primitive nth roots of unity" / "totient of n" / "count integers coprime to n / relatively prime to n"** -> **phi(n)**.

Don't derive under the buzzer — recognize the phrase, fire the matching one-liner. The knight/soldier/egg word-problems ARE CRT in disguise; "rows of k, r left over" means x = r (mod k).

cards.title: CRT fast: two golden patterns writers build in
cards.body:
System x = r_i (mod n_i), pairwise-coprime n_i, has a **unique** solution mod L = lcm(n_i). Build by successive substitution, NEVER search.

**Pattern A - same deficit (the big one):** if r_i = n_i - d for every i (each remainder short of its divisor by the SAME d), then x = -d (mod L), so **answer = L - d**. *Why:* x = -d (mod n_i) means n_i | (x+d) for all i, so L | (x+d), so x = -d (mod L). One line.

**Pattern B - same remainder:** if r_i = r for every i, then x = r (mod L); smallest such x is r itself (or r + L if they want the next one). *Why:* same argument on (x - r).

Writers construct most Science Bowl CRT tossups to hit Pattern A or B, so check the gaps FIRST before touching substitution.

cards.title: Your placement CRT in 5s (not 41s)
cards.body:
*2023-r10-t23: x=3 mod5, 2 mod4, 1 mod3.* Check the gaps: 5-3=2, 4-2=2, 3-1=2 — all short by **2**. So x = -2 (mod lcm(5,4,3)=60) -> x = 60-2 = **58**. Done. Verify once: 58 = 55+3, 56+2, 57+1. Buzz.

Same Pattern A, 2025-r4-t21 (knights): rows of 4 leave 2, 5 leave 3, 7 leave 5 -> deficits 2,2,2 -> lcm(4,5,7)=140 -> 140-2 = **138**.

**No clean pattern?** Merge two at a time: x=1 mod3 & x=3 mod5 -> x=13 mod15; then 13+15k = 2 (mod4) -> 1+3k = 2 -> 3k = 1 (mod4) -> k=3 -> 58. Substitution beats scanning a list every time.

cards.title: WHY Legendre's floor-sum works
cards.body:
Exponent of prime p in N! = floor(N/p) + floor(N/p^2) + floor(N/p^3) + ...

*Reconstruct it:* among 1..N there are floor(N/p) multiples of p, each donating **at least one** factor p — that's the first term. Multiples of p^2 donate a *second* p that the first count missed, so add floor(N/p^2). Multiples of p^3 donate a third — add floor(N/p^3). You are counting each copy of p exactly once, tier by tier, never double-counting. Stop when p^k > N (that floor is 0).

cards.title: Trailing zeros of N! in ANY base b
cards.body:
Factor b = product of p^{a_p}. For each prime, get e_p = its Legendre exponent in N!. **Trailing zeros = min over p of floor(e_p / a_p).**

*Why min:* one trailing zero = one factor of b, and b needs a_p copies of each prime p, so you're bottlenecked by the scarcest prime. *Why the floor-divide:* e_p copies of p make only floor(e_p/a_p) complete groups of a_p.

- Base 3 (prime), 30!: e_3 = 10+3+1 = **14** (single prime, no divide; 2023-r3-t20).
- Base 2, 17!: e_2 = 8+4+2+1 = **15** (binary trailing zeros).
- Base 8 = 2^3, 20!: e_2 = 10+5+2+1 = 18, floor(18/3) = **6** (2025-r4-b14).
- Base 10 = 2*5, N!: e_5 < e_2 always, so trailing zeros = e_5 = floor(N/5)+floor(N/25)+... (the classic).

cards.title: WHY primitive nth roots = phi(n)  <- your miss
cards.body:
The nth roots of unity are e^{2*pi*i*k/n}, k = 0..n-1. One is **primitive** iff its powers generate *all* n roots — equivalently the fraction k/n is already in lowest terms, i.e. **gcd(k,n)=1**. Counting k in 1..n with gcd(k,n)=1 is exactly the definition of phi(n).

n=12: k in {1,5,7,11} -> **4** primitive roots. You guessed 2 — the eyeball trap (people picture only +/- of a couple obvious ones). Always compute phi. phi(12) = 12*(1-1/2)*(1-1/3) = 12*(1/2)*(2/3) = **4**.

cards.title: Totient phi(n) — compute in 3 seconds
cards.body:
phi(n) = n * product of (1 - 1/p) over the **distinct** primes p dividing n.

*Why the product:* start with n candidates; for each prime p|n, a fraction 1/p of them are multiples of p and get killed, leaving (1-1/p). Multiplicativity across distinct primes folds inclusion-exclusion in automatically — no overlap correction needed.

Speed facts: phi(p) = p-1 (prime); phi(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1} = p^{k-1}(p-1); phi is multiplicative on coprime parts, so phi(12) = phi(4)*phi(3) = 2*2 = 4. **Largest phi over 1..100 = phi(97) = 96** (largest prime <= 100; phi(p)=p-1 and no composite near 100 beats it — phi(99)=60, phi(98)=42, phi(100)=40).

cards.title: Roots-of-unity distractor: product is NOT always 1
cards.body:
The nth roots of unity always **sum to 0**, but their **product = (-1)^{n+1}** (i.e. +1 if n odd, -1 if n even). n=2: roots 1, -1, product = -1. That's why 2024-r9-t12's answer ("not necessarily true") is *"the roots have a product of one"* — it fails for every even n.

*Why:* the roots are the zeros of x^n - 1, so their product = (-1)^n * (constant/leading) = (-1)^n * (-1) = (-1)^{n+1}.

Traps in that same question that ARE always true (so NOT the answer): sum of roots = 0, sum of real parts = 0, and product of imaginary parts = 0 (the root 1 has imaginary part 0, forcing the product to 0).

cards.title: Adjacent reflexes the bank reuses
cards.body:
**Nontotients ("cannot be a totient"):** phi(n) is even for all n>2, so every **odd number > 1** is a nontotient instantly. If the choices are all even (e.g. 42,46,50,54 in 2024-r10-b23), that filter fails — then use: m is a totient if m+1 is prime (m = phi(m+1)) or m = phi(prime power). 42=phi(43), 46=phi(47), 54=phi(81); **50 has no preimage -> answer 50**. Smallest even nontotients to know: 14, 26, 34, 38, 50.

**Modular inverse:** 1/9 mod13 -> 9x=1 -> x=3 (9*3=27=26+1). 34^{-1} mod37: 34 = -3, so -3x=1 -> 3x=36 -> x=**12**. Use small negatives.

**Wilson:** (p-1)! = -1 (mod p). So 11! mod13: 12! = -1 and 12 = -1, hence 11! = (-1)/(-1) = **1**.

**Sum of divisors of 2^k:** sigma(2^k) = 2^{k+1} - 1, so sigma(1024) = 2^11 - 1 = **2047**.

This lesson makes cos(2x) a 2-second reflex you regenerate from ONE formula (cos²−sin²) plus a Pythagorean swap, so you never freeze on the choice again.
overview: Trig identities in this bank are almost never \"prove an identity\" — they're **speed traps**: handed one trig value and asked for cos(2x), a messy expression that collapses to a single function, or a max/area that hides a double-angle. The writers reward whoever has `cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1` and `sin²x + cos²x = 1` as pure reflex. Winning mindset: **don't find the angle** — match the double-angle form to the value you were given and write it before the moderator finishes. Everything here regenerates from just two facts (Pythagorean + one double-angle form), so you never stall picking a formula.

cards.title: What this topic actually looks like at the buzzer
cards.body:
Trig identities in the Math bank are almost never "prove an identity." They're **speed traps** built on 4 recurring sub-patterns:

1. **Given one value, find cos(2x)/sin(2x)** — the classic (2023-r1-b10, YOUR question). Pure reflex.
2. **Collapse a messy expression to one function** — `cot x · sin²x / cos x` → `sin x` (2025-r5-t3). Rewrite everything in sin/cos and cancel.
3. **Hidden double-angle in a max/area problem** — legs sin x, cos x → area = ½ sin x cos x = ¼ sin 2x (2023-r11-t13).
4. **Pythagorean bridge between sec/csc/sin/cos**, often as an if-and-only-if (2025-r6-t24 → a = √2).

All four run on the **same two facts**: `sin²x + cos²x = 1` and `cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x`. Own those and the whole topic is free points — no angle-solving, ever.

cards.title: WHY sin²x + cos²x = 1 — it IS the Pythagorean theorem
cards.body:
On the unit circle, the point at angle x is **(cos x, sin x)** by definition. It lies on a circle of radius 1, so its distance from the origin is 1. Distance formula: `cos²x + sin²x = 1²`. That's the whole proof — the Pythagorean *identity* is the Pythagorean *theorem* on a radius-1 triangle.

This is your **regenerator**: blank on anything, rebuild from here.
- Divide the whole thing by cos²x → `1 + tan²x = sec²x`
- Divide by sin²x → `1 + cot²x = csc²x`

Never memorize those last two as separate rows — they're one division away.

cards.title: WHY the three cos(2x) forms are really ONE formula
cards.body:
Start from angle addition `cos(A+B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B`, set A = B = x:

`cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x`  ← the ONLY row to actually remember

Swap the sines out with `sin²x = 1 − cos²x`:
`= cos²x − (1 − cos²x) = 2cos²x − 1`

Swap the cosines out with `cos²x = 1 − sin²x`:
`= (1 − sin²x) − sin²x = 1 − 2sin²x`

So the "three identities you forgot" are **one identity + one Pythagorean swap.** Given a cosine → cos-only form; given a sine → sin-only form. You regenerate whichever you need in 3 seconds. **This is the direct fix for your +38s** — you don't recall a row, you rebuild it.

cards.title: The double-angle trio (memorize the reasons, not the rows)
cards.body:
- `cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x` — *one formula; the last two are the Pythagorean swap (previous card).*
- `sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x` — *from sin(A+B)=sinA cosB+cosA sinB with A=B: the two cross-terms sinx·cosx are identical, so they add to 2 sinx cosx.*
- **Pick by what you're handed:** have cos → `2cos²−1`; have sin → `1−2sin²`; need sin 2x → you need BOTH sin and cos (recover the missing one via the 3-4-5 / Pythagorean).

*Sanity check any form at x=45°:* cos90=0, and 2cos²45−1 = 2·½−1 = 0 ✓. Verified numerically.

cards.title: Amplitude, power-reduction, tan-addition (each with its reason)
cards.body:
- **Amplitude:** `a sin x + b cos x` has max `√(a²+b²)`, min `−√(a²+b²)`. *Why: it equals R·sin(x+φ) with R=√(a²+b²), since a=R cosφ, b=R sinφ and a²+b²=R²(cos²+sin²)=R². A sine wave peaks at its amplitude R. Directly nails 2023-r8-t13: max of e^(sinx+cosx)=e^√2.*
- **Power reduction:** `cos²x = (1+cos2x)/2`, `sin²x = (1−cos2x)/2`. *Why: just solve `2cos²−1=cos2x` and `1−2sin²=cos2x` for cos²/sin². Rearrangements, not new facts.*
- **Tangent addition:** `tan(A+B) = (tanA+tanB)/(1−tanA·tanB)`. *Why: take sin(A+B)/cos(A+B) and divide top and bottom by cosA·cosB — every term becomes a tangent. Powers arctan sums (2024-r10-b3).*

cards.title: Buzzer word → weapon
cards.body:
- **"cos(2x)" / "sin(2x)"** + a given value → double-angle reflex; do NOT solve for x.
- **"simplest form" / "in terms of a single trig function"** → rewrite all in sin & cos, cancel.
- **"largest / maximum area"** with a sin·cos product → it's ½ sin 2x, so max = ½ of the coefficient (½·½ = ¼ here).
- **"maximum of a sin x + b cos x"** (or e^that, or anything monotonic of it) → √(a²+b²).
- **sec/csc/tan/cot mixed with "if and only if"** → convert to sin/cos, force the two conditions equal via sin²+cos²=1.
- **"cosine of 0.02" / any tiny angle / limit as x→0** → small-angle: cos θ≈1−θ²/2, sin θ≈θ, tan θ≈θ.

cards.title: Your placement question, the 2-second way
cards.body:
**2023-r1-b10: cos x = 3/5, find cos 2x.**

Trigger fires the instant you hear "cos 2x" with a **cosine** given → grab the **cos-only form** `2cos²x − 1`:
`2·(3/5)² − 1 = 18/25 − 25/25 = −7/25.` (verified)

Done. No x, no arccos, no deliberating between forms — that deliberation was your 38-second leak.

**If they'd asked sin 2x instead:** you'd need sin x too. cos=3/5 is a 3-4-5 triangle → sin=4/5, so sin 2x = 2·(3/5)(4/5) = **24/25**.

cards.title: The traps (including the one that cost you 38s)
cards.body:
- **Your leak:** trying to recover x, or freezing while you decide which cos-2x form is "right." Don't decide — **match the form to the given value** (cos→cos-form, sin→sin-form) and go. Blank? Rebuild from `cos²−sin²` + Pythagorean.
- **Sign trap:** it's `2cos²−1` (minus one), NOT `2cos²+1`. Writing `1−2cos²x` by mistake gives **+7/25** — the exact distractor. Verified: 1−2(9/25)=+7/25. Guard with x=90°: cos180=−1=2·0−1 ✓.
- **sin 2x needs the sign of the missing function.** cos=3/5 allows sin=±4/5 if no quadrant is given; bank problems usually imply acute → take positive.
- **Amplitude ≠ a+b.** Max of sinx+cosx is √2 ≈ 1.41 (the hypotenuse), NOT 2 (the sum). Classic distractor.

cards.title: Small-angle shortcuts (a live bank pattern)
cards.body:
For tiny θ in **radians**: `sin θ ≈ θ`, `tan θ ≈ θ`, `cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2`.

*Why:* a tiny arc of length θ on the unit circle is almost a straight vertical segment of height sin θ, so sin θ ≈ θ. cos θ dips below 1 by the second-order amount θ²/2 (the leading Taylor correction).

Bank hits: `cos(0.02) ≈ 1 − (0.02)²/2 = 1 − 0.0002 = 0.9998` (2025-r12-b1, verified). And `lim_{x→0} sin7x/sin4x = 7/4`, since sin7x≈7x, sin4x≈4x and the x cancels (verified 1.75). The instant you hear "small angle" or "limit as x→0," replace each sin/tan by its argument.

practice.note: Hidden double-angle inside an area problem — the trap is grinding calculus or AM-GM. Spot the sin·cos product and it's instant.
practice.solution: Right-triangle legs sin x, cos x → area = ½·sin x·cos x = ¼·(2 sin x cos x) = ¼ sin 2x. Max of sin 2x is 1 (at x=45°, where both legs are positive), so max area = **1/4** (verified). No calculus needed.

practice.note: Pythagorean-bridge / iff problem. Convert sec→cos, csc→sin, then force the two conditions to be the SAME set for all θ using sin²+cos²=1. Harder — a good bonus-pace target.
practice.solution: |sec θ|>a ⟺ |cos θ|<1/a ⟺ cos²θ<1/a² ⟺ 1−sin²θ<1/a² ⟺ sin²θ > 1−1/a². And |csc θ|<a ⟺ |sin θ|>1/a ⟺ sin²θ > 1/a². The biconditional holds for EVERY θ iff the two thresholds coincide: 1−1/a² = 1/a² ⟹ 1 = 2/a² ⟹ a² = 2 ⟹ a = **√2** (brute-force checked over 10⁵ angles: holds). Needs a>0.

practice.note: Tangent-addition powers arctan sums. Fastest recognition: the classic identity arctan1+arctan2+arctan3 = 180°, so arctan2+arctan3 = 180°−45° = 135° with zero computation. The tan-formula route is the backup.
practice.solution: Fast: arctan1+arctan2+arctan3 = 180° (verified) ⟹ arctan2+arctan3 = 180−45 = **135**. Backup: tan(arctan2+arctan3) = (2+3)/(1−2·3) = 5/(−5) = −1; both arctans lie in (0°,90°) so their sum is in (90°,180°), and the angle there with tan = −1 is 135°.

practice.note: Amplitude identity hidden under an exponential. e^u is increasing, so just maximize the exponent u = sin x + cos x.

why: On placement Q7 (2024-r14-t12) you buzzed 72 — the value of A·B that the problem GAVE you — when it asked for |A×B| = 96. You knew the numbers but grabbed the wrong product. This lesson drills the one reflex that fixes it: the given product and the asked product are different legs of the same right triangle, so a given A·B never IS the answer — you still owe the identity.
overview: Only ~8 vectors questions live in this bank, and they cluster into three tight patterns: **orthogonality** (dot = 0, solve for an unknown component — 3 questions, the most common), the **cross-magnitude identity** (given |A|,|B|,A·B → find |A×B| — 2 questions, and the one you missed), and **magnitude of a sum** (law of cosines from the dot product). The unifying trick for the cross pattern: **never solve for θ.** Treat |A||B| as a hypotenuse and the two products |A·B|, |A×B| as its legs, spot the Pythagorean triple (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) hiding in the numbers, and read the answer off in ~2 seconds. For orthogonality, write the componentwise sum and set it to zero. That's the whole event.

cards.title: The two products, side by side
cards.body:
For vectors A, B with angle θ between them:

- **A·B = |A||B|cosθ** (a scalar)
- **|A×B| = |A||B|sinθ** (magnitude of a vector)

**Why paired:** same |A||B| in front, one carries cos, one carries sin. Dot measures *alignment* (max when parallel, θ=0), cross measures *spread/area* (max when perpendicular, θ=90°). As θ turns, they trade off — and because cos²+sin²=1, they can't both be large. That trade-off IS the identity on the next card.

cards.title: THE identity — why |A×B|²=|A|²|B|²−(A·B)² is just cos²+sin²=1
cards.body:
**|A×B|² = |A|²|B|² − (A·B)²**

**Two-line derivation:** (A·B)² = |A|²|B|²cos²θ and |A×B|² = |A|²|B|²sin²θ. Add them → |A|²|B|²(cos²θ+sin²θ) = |A|²|B|². Subtract (A·B)² to isolate |A×B|². Done — this is Lagrange's identity.

**Mental picture:** the product |A||B| is a hypotenuse; |A·B| and |A×B| are its two legs. **cos²+sin²=1 becomes leg²+leg²=hyp².** You never touch θ, arccos, or a calculator.

cards.title: 'magnitudes given + one product given → find the OTHER product'
cards.body:
The trigger words: **'have magnitudes … If A·B = … what is the magnitude of A×B'** (or the reverse). The instant you see |A|, |B|, and ONE product, asked for the OTHER → **|A×B|² = |A|²|B|² − (A·B)²**. Both bank instances: 2024-r14-t12, 2025-r10-t1.

**Two hard rules that fix your miss:** (1) **Do NOT find θ.** (2) The given product is never the answer — it's the bait sitting in the problem. **Sign of A·B is irrelevant** — it gets squared, so A·B = −72 behaves exactly like +72.

cards.title: Spot the hidden triple (skip all squaring)
cards.body:
Writers engineer these as scaled Pythagorean triples: hyp = |A||B|, one leg = |A·B|, other leg = |A×B|. Train your eye on **3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17**.

**Placement Q7 (2024-r14-t12):** |A||B| = 8·15 = 120, |A·B| = |−72| = 72. See **72, ?, 120 = 24·(3,4,5)** → missing leg = 24·4 = **96**. ~2s, no squaring.

**2025-r10-t1:** |A||B| = 20·25 = 500, |A·B| = 400. **400, ?, 500 = 100·(4,3,5)** → |A×B| = 100·3 = **300**.

If no triple appears, fall back to √(|A|²|B|² − (A·B)²) — but check for the triple first.

cards.title: Orthogonality = dot product zero (the MOST common vector Q)
cards.body:
**A ⊥ B ⟺ A·B = 0.** In components, A·B = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.

**Why:** A·B = |A||B|cosθ and cos90° = 0, so 'perpendicular' and 'dot = 0' are literally the same statement.

**Method:** write the componentwise sum, set = 0, solve for the unknown. **Watch for a dropped component** — if one vector is written 3î − 4k̂, its ĵ-coefficient is 0, so that whole term vanishes. This family is the bank's biggest (2023-r7-t10, 2024-r3-t19, 2023-r7-b6 — that last one goes quadratic).

cards.title: |A±B|² — the law of cosines, straight from the dot product
cards.body:
**|A+B|² = |A|² + |B|² + 2(A·B)**  (flip the middle sign for |A−B|²)

**Derivation:** |A+B|² = (A+B)·(A+B) = A·A + 2A·B + B·B = |A|² + |B|² + 2A·B, using A·A = |A|². The cross-term 2A·B = 2|A||B|cosθ is exactly the −2ab·cos(C) correction in the law of cosines — the dot product IS the law of cosines.

**2025-r13-b13:** |a|=6, |b|=8, a·b=16 → 36 + 64 + 2(16) = 132 → |a+b| = √132 = **2√33**. Leave it as a simplified radical.

cards.title: Cross product ⊥ BOTH inputs — and the true/false distractors
cards.body:
A×B ⊥ A and A×B ⊥ B, always. The bank tests this as a true/false triple (2024-r12-t10):
- **A·(A×B) = 0** → TRUE. *Why:* it's the scalar triple product = det[A;A;B], a determinant with a repeated row, which is 0.
- **A×A = 0** vector → TRUE (θ=0, sinθ=0).
- **A·A = |A|² ≠ 0** for nonzero A → **FALSE**, the classic bait (θ=0, cos0=1).

Also know the symmetries: **A×B = −(B×A)** (anti-commutative), **A·B = B·A** (commutative).

cards.title: Area = ½|A×B|, and the ratio-scaling calc trick
cards.body:
|A×B| = **parallelogram** area on A,B; half of it = **triangle area = ½|A||B|sinθ** — same sinθ, disguised.

**2024-r11-t8** hands you a reference (sides 3,4 at 1° → area 0.10) and asks sides 2,18 at 2°. Don't recompute — **scale the reference**: new/ref = (2·18)/(3·4) × (sin2°/sin1°) = 3 × 2 = 6, so area = 6 × 0.10 = **0.6**. The sin2°/sin1° ≈ 2 comes from small-angle sinθ≈θ; the reference exists precisely so you never touch a calculator.

cards.title: Your exact miss: they asked cross, you gave dot
cards.body:
On placement Q7 (2024-r14-t12) you answered **72 = |A·B|** — but that value was GIVEN, and the question asked **|A×B| = 96**. Because both numbers live in the same problem, the wrong one is always sitting right there as bait.

**Fixed reflex:** a given product is a *leg*, never the answer — if A·B is handed to you, you still owe √(|A|²|B|² − (A·B)²) (or spot the triple). And square out the sign immediately: the −72 in that problem is just 72 for this purpose.

Different type — magnitude of a SUM. Use the law-of-cosines expansion; do NOT find θ. Bonus (~20s), so leave a simplified radical.

practice.note: Harder orthogonality — the unknown appears nonlinearly, giving a quadratic in u = a². 'Largest possible real value' selects the positive root, and don't forget the final √.
practice.solution: Dot = a·a + a²·a² + (2)(−3) = a⁴ + a² − 6 = 0. Let u = a²: u² + u − 6 = (u+3)(u−2) = 0 → u = 2 (u = −3 rejected). a = ±√2 → largest = **√2**.

why: On the placement you missed 2023-r9-b23 ("closest point on y=2x−3 to the origin") by "guessing the intercept." The whole trap is that the closest point is NOT an intercept — it's the foot of a perpendicular. This lesson makes dropping that perpendicular a 5-second reflex.
overview: This bank leans hard on ONE idea dressed four ways: the closest point on a line/curve is where the segment to it is **perpendicular** to the line (or to the tangent). It appears as "closest point on a line to the origin" (2023-r9-b23), "line perpendicular to a curve at a point" i.e. the normal line (2023-r8-b23), "at the closest point, tangent slope" (2024-r7-b21), and "circle tangent to a line → radius ⟂ tangent" (2025-r15-t13). Fast mindset: the instant you hear *closest / nearest / perpendicular / tangent / normal*, reach for **negative-reciprocal slope** and **drop a perpendicular** — never read off an intercept, never reach for calculus if a slope trick will do.

cards.title: WHY closest point = foot of perpendicular
cards.body: Pick any point Q on the line. The segment from your point P to Q is the hypotenuse of a right triangle: one leg is the fixed perpendicular distance from P to the line, the other leg runs *along* the line. Hypotenuse² = (perp leg)² + (along leg)². The perp leg is constant, so PQ shrinks only by killing the along-line leg — and it hits zero exactly when PQ ⟂ line. So **closest ⟺ perpendicular**. Reconstruct this once and you will never guess an intercept again.

cards.title: WHY the foot-from-origin formula works (2-line derivation)
cards.body: Line ax+by+c=0 has normal vector (a,b). From the origin the foot must lie straight out along that normal, so foot = t·(a,b). Plug into the line: a(ta)+b(tb)+c=0 → t(a²+b²)=−c → **t=−c/(a²+b²)**. Hence foot=(−ac/(a²+b²), −bc/(a²+b²)), and distance=|t|·√(a²+b²)=|c|/√(a²+b²). You derived BOTH the closest point and the distance in two lines — no black box.

cards.title: Perpendicular slope = negative reciprocal (−1/m)
cards.body: A line of slope m has perpendiculars of slope **−1/m**. WHY: rotating a direction 90° sends (Δx,Δy)→(−Δy,Δx), so m=Δy/Δx becomes Δx/(−Δy)=−1/m. This one fact powers 'perpendicular to a curve' (flip the tangent slope), circle tangents (⟂ radius), and normal lines. Edge case: horizontal (m=0) ⟂ vertical (undefined slope) — the formula 'breaks' precisely there, so watch for it.

cards.title: Distance from a point to a line
cards.body: Distance from (x₀,y₀) to ax+by+c=0 = **|a·x₀+b·y₀+c| / √(a²+b²)**. WHY: a·x₀+b·y₀+c is how far (x₀,y₀) sits off the line measured along the normal (a,b); dividing by |(a,b)|=√(a²+b²) rescales that to true length. From the origin it collapses to **|c|/√(a²+b²)**. MUST convert to ax+by+c=0 first (y=2x−3 → 2x−y−3=0).

cards.title: Foot of perpendicular from the ORIGIN
cards.body: To ax+by+c=0: foot = **(−ac/(a²+b²), −bc/(a²+b²)) = (−c/(a²+b²))·(a,b)**. So the foot is always a **scalar multiple of the normal (a,b)** — instant sanity check. For y=2x−3 → 2x−y−3=0 (a=2,b=−1,c=−3): t=3/5, foot=(3/5)(2,−1)=(6/5,−3/5). If you blank on the formula, use the hand-method below — it's actually faster.

cards.title: Vector projection (the general engine)
cards.body: Component of v along direction u: **proj = (v·u / u·u)·u**. WHY: v·u=|v||u|cosθ measures overlap; dividing by |u|²=u·u rescales u to exactly the right length. Closest point of P on a line through A with direction u is **A + proj of (P−A) onto u**. Every closest-point result on this list is a special case of this — worth knowing when the line doesn't pass through a clean point.

cards.title: Exact words that scream 'drop a perpendicular'
cards.body: From the real bank: *'closest to the origin'*, *'closest point on the line'*, *'perpendicular to the curve of … at the point'*, *'tangent to a line at (point)'*, *'the point at which … is closest to the origin … slope of the tangent line'*. Reflex: negative-reciprocal slope + intersect, OR point-to-line distance formula. Also *nearest*, *shortest distance*, *normal line*, *radius ⟂ tangent*.

cards.title: FAST path — closest point on a line to the origin (safest buzzer method)
cards.body: 'Closest point on y=2x−3 to origin.' Perpendicular through origin has slope −1/2 → y=−x/2. Set equal: −x/2=2x−3 → −x=4x−6 → 5x=6 → x=6/5, y=−3/5. **(6/5,−3/5)** in ~5s. Two lines of algebra, no formula to misremember. Sanity check: (6/5,−3/5) is (3/5)(2,−1) = scalar × normal. ✓

cards.title: FAST path — circle tangent to a line at a point
cards.body: Center (1,8), tangent at (0,6). Radius slope=(6−8)/(0−1)=2. Tangent ⟂ radius → slope −1/2. Line through (0,6): y=−x/2+6. x-intercept: 0=−x/2+6 → x=**12**. One trick (tangent ⟂ radius) does the whole thing. Speed cue: the tangent point IS a point on the line, so you get the line free once you have the slope.

cards.title: YOUR placement miss: the closest point is NOT an intercept
cards.body: On 2023-r9-b23 you guessed the intercept. The y-intercept (0,−3) and x-intercept (1.5,0) are just axis crossings — they are almost never the closest point to the origin (they only would be for a horizontal/vertical line). The closest point is the FOOT OF THE PERPENDICULAR: drop a ⟂ from the origin. Second trap: forgetting to convert to ax+by+c=0 before a formula (y=2x−3 → 2x−y−3=0, so c=−3, not +3 — a sign slip flips your whole answer).

cards.title: MC distractor pattern on the tangent/closest problems
cards.body: On 2024-r7-b21 the choices are W)−2 X)−0.5 Y)0.5 Z)2. The traps are engineered from the radius slope (−1/2): **X)−0.5 is the radius slope itself** (bait if you forget to flip), Y)0.5 is a sign error, W)−2 is negative-reciprocal-with-wrong-sign. The answer Z)2 is the true negative reciprocal. Rule: compute the radius/segment slope, then confidently pick its negative reciprocal — the given slope is always sitting there as a trap.
