practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT MISS. 'Closest point on y=2x−3 to the origin.' You guessed the intercept — the answer is the foot of the perpendicular. Do NOT read off a crossing.
practice.solution: Perpendicular from origin to a line of slope 2 has slope −1/2: y=−x/2. Set equal to the line: −x/2 = 2x−3 → −x = 4x−6 → 5x=6 → x=6/5, y=2(6/5)−3=−3/5. Answer **(6/5, −3/5)**. Formula check: 2x−y−3=0 → a=2,b=−1,c=−3, a²+b²=5, t=−c/5=3/5, foot=(3/5)(2,−1)=(6/5,−3/5). ✓

practice.note: 'Line perpendicular to y=x² at (2,4)' = the normal line. Get the tangent slope by derivative, flip to negative reciprocal, then point-slope. Answer must be in slope-intercept form.
practice.solution: Slope of y=x² is 2x; at x=2 that's 4. Perpendicular (normal) slope = −1/4. Through (2,4): y−4=−¼(x−2) → y=−¼x+½+4 = **y = −¼x + 9/2**. ✓

practice.note: The elegant version of the same principle: at the point on a curve CLOSEST to the origin, the segment from the origin is ⟂ to the tangent. You never need a, b, or c — don't get baited into 'finding the quadratic.'
practice.solution: Closest point is (1/2, −1/4). Slope of the segment from origin = (−1/4)/(1/2) = −1/2. Tangent ⟂ segment → tangent slope = −1/(−1/2) = **2** (choice Z). Trap check: X)−0.5 is the segment slope itself, the classic 'forgot to flip' bait. ✓

practice.note: 'Circle tangent to a line at a point' → tangent ⟂ radius. (Bank note: this id also tags an unrelated Eulerian-path visual; the circle-tangent question is the one here, stored answer 12.) Watch the radius direction and finish by solving for the x-intercept.
practice.solution: Radius from center (1,8) to tangent point (0,6): slope=(6−8)/(0−1)=2. Tangent slope=−1/2. The line passes through the tangent point (0,6): y=−½x+6. Set y=0: x=**12**. ✓

practice.note: Line-meets-curve, the anti-'guess-the-intercept' drill: you must SET the equations equal, not read a crossing. Then Vieta beats solving for the roots.
practice.solution: y=x²+9x meets y=36: x²+9x−36=0. Sum of the two x-coordinates = −(coeff of x)/(leading coeff) = −9/1 = **−9** (Vieta — no need to factor or find each root). ✓

why: On Q14 (2024-r6-b18) you set d=rt up backwards: you didn't lock in that the SLOWER 80-mph trip eats MORE time, so your subtraction pointed the wrong way and the sign flipped. The correct line is x/80 − x/90 = 1/6 → x = 120. This lesson drills the "which time is bigger" reflex so the direction is automatic before you touch algebra.
overview: In this bank, rate/word problems are almost never about physics — they're about setting up ONE clean equation fast without flipping a sign or a unit. The recurring flavors: (1) same distance, two speeds, given a TIME GAP (your Q14); (2) same TIME, two speeds → distances split in the speed ratio; (3) combined-work "rates add"; (4) average speed = total distance / total time (a trap that punishes averaging the speeds); (5) return-to-START = LCM of round-trip times; (6) percent-stacking (multiply factors). The winning mindset: before algebra, say "faster → less time" and decide which quantity is LARGER. That one sentence fixes the direction of the subtraction, and the rest is arithmetic you can do on the buzzer — often via a closed form with no algebra at all.

cards.title: The one frame: t = d/r, then ask 'which is bigger?'
cards.body: Every d=rt problem is the same triangle: **d = r·t**, so **t = d/r** and **r = d/t**. Pick the variable to ISOLATE; the other two are given or expressible. The whole game on a timed buzzer: *before* writing anything, name which time (or distance) is LARGER. Same distance, faster speed → smaller time. Same speed, longer distance → larger time. Deciding this first tells you which term leads a subtraction — the exact step you missed on Q14.

cards.title: WHY faster = less time (so you never flip the setup)
cards.body: t = d/r puts rate in the **denominator**, so a bigger rate makes the fraction *smaller*. Concretely for 120 mi: at 90 mph, 120/90 = 4/3 hr; at 80 mph, 120/80 = 3/2 hr. The slower (80) trip takes longer. So 'faster arrives EARLIER by Δt' means **(slower time) − (faster time) = Δt** — bigger minus smaller = positive gap. Rescue line to say out loud on the buzzer: 'slower is 80, slower = MORE time, so x/80 comes first.' That single sentence is the entire fix for your Q14 miss.

cards.title: Time-gap setup — and the no-algebra closed form
cards.body:
Same distance d, two speeds, faster saves time Δt:

**d/r_slow − d/r_fast = Δt**

Each term is literally a travel time (t=d/r); slower rate → bigger d/r, so slower-minus-faster is the positive Δt. **Solve it in your head with the closed form:** combine over r_slow·r_fast to get d·(r_fast − r_slow)/(r_slow·r_fast) = Δt, so

**d = Δt · r_slow · r_fast / (r_fast − r_slow)**.

Q14: (1/6)(80)(90)/(90−80) = (1/6)(7200)/10 = 120 — zero algebra. **Unit gotcha:** speeds are per HOUR, gaps come in MINUTES — convert (10 min = 1/6 hr) *before* plugging in.

cards.title: Average speed = total distance / total time (NOT the mean of speeds)
cards.body:
For a trip in pieces at different speeds:

**v̄ = (total distance) / (total time) = Σdᵢ / Σ(dᵢ/vᵢ)**

Why never average speeds: only TIMES add along a trip, so sum each leg's time dᵢ/vᵢ, then divide total distance by it. **Equal-distance** legs collapse to the harmonic mean 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂), always *below* (v₁+v₂)/2 — that arithmetic mean is the baited wrong answer. Example (2025-r7-b12): distance D, 98% at 1 m/s + 2% at 0.5 m/s → time = 0.98D + 0.02D/0.5 = 0.98D + 0.04D = 1.02D → v̄ = D/1.02D = **50/51**.

cards.title: Combined work: rates ADD
cards.body: A finishes in a minutes, B in b minutes → rates 1/a and 1/b jobs/min; **together 1/a + 1/b**, so time = **ab/(a+b)**. Why: in one minute the work done is A's chunk PLUS B's chunk — amounts of work are additive, so per-minute rates add. N identical workers scale the rate by N. Fast check (2023-r2-b18): 1 farmer = 5 acres/10 min = 0.5 acre/min; 5 farmers = 2.5 acre/min; 50 ÷ 2.5 = **20 min** (or: 5 farmers do 25 acres in 10 min, so 50 acres = 20 min).

cards.title: Same TIME → distances split in the speed ratio
cards.body: Two movers traveling the SAME duration t: d = r·t makes distance ∝ speed, so **d_A/d_B = r_A/r_B** — you never solve for t. Q 2024-r10-t3: 'Alice finishes as Bob STARTS his 5th lap' means Bob has DONE 4 laps = 1600 m while Alice does 2000 m in the same t, so speeds are 2000:1600 = 5:4. Alice is 1 m/s faster: a/(a−1) = 5/4 → 4a = 5a−5 → a = 5 m/s → t = 2000/5 = **400 s**. No simultaneous equations.

cards.title: Return to the START = LCM of ROUND-TRIP times
cards.body: 'Next time they meet at the starting point' = both simultaneously complete a whole number of ROUND trips. A round trip = 2× the one-way time, so take the LCM of the ROUND-trip times. Q 2025-r2-b24: one-way 30 and 40 → round trips 60 and 80 → LCM(60,80) = **240 s**. The trap answer LCM(30,40)=120 uses one-way times; at t=120 Alice is at the start wall (4 lengths) but Bob is at the FAR wall (3 lengths) — they aren't even together, let alone at the start. (Meeting *anywhere*, e.g. head-on mid-pool, is a different, harder question — read the prompt for 'at the starting point'.)

cards.title: Keyword → technique reflex
cards.body:
- 'arrives ___ earlier/later', 'if she'd gone X instead of Y' → **d/r_slow − d/r_fast = Δt** (or closed form d = Δt·r_slow·r_fast/(r_fast−r_slow))
- 'finishes just as the other…', 'at the same time' → **distances ∝ speeds**
- 'together', 'both pipes/farmers', 'how long to fill' → **rates add, ab/(a+b)**
- 'average speed over the whole trip' → **total dist / total time** (do NOT average speeds)
- 'meet at the starting point again' → **LCM of round-trip (2×) times**
- 'increases X% then decreases Y%', 'both coupons' → **multiply the factors**

cards.title: Q14 worked at buzzer speed
cards.body: '90 mph arrives 10 min earlier than 80 mph; how far?' Say the sentence: *slower is 80 → 80 gets the bigger time.* Convert: 10 min = 1/6 hr. **Fastest path (no algebra):** d = Δt·r_slow·r_fast/(r_fast−r_slow) = (1/6)(80·90)/10 = 1200/10 = **120 mi**. Algebra path if you blank on the formula: x/80 − x/90 = 1/6, clear by LCM(80,90)=720 → 9x − 8x = 120 → x = 120. Check: 120/80 = 1.5 hr vs 120/90 ≈ 1.333 hr → 1/6 hr = 10 min earlier. ✓

cards.title: The three traps that cost points
cards.body: 1. **Backwards subtraction (your Q14):** x/90 − x/80 gives −1/6 → x = −120. Guard: name the slower trip as the bigger time FIRST, or use the closed form (denominator r_fast − r_slow is automatically positive). 2. **Unit mismatch:** mph with a gap in minutes — convert minutes to hours (÷60) before solving; skipping it turns Δt=1/6 into 10. 3. **Averaging speeds:** round trips / equal legs give the harmonic mean (below the arithmetic mean); (v₁+v₂)/2 is the classic bait.

practice.solution: 1 farmer: 5 acres / 10 min = 0.5 acre/min. 5 farmers: 2.5 acre/min. 50 acres ÷ 2.5 = **20 min**. Shortcut: 5 farmers plow 25 acres in 10 min, so 50 acres takes 20 min.

practice.note: Same-TIME pattern — distances split in the speed ratio, so you never solve a system for t. 'Starts his 5th lap' means Bob has COMPLETED 4 laps = 1600 m, not 5 — misread this and you get 5:5.
practice.solution: In the same time t, Alice runs 2000 m, Bob runs 4·400 = 1600 m, so speeds are 2000:1600 = 5:4. Alice is 1 m/s faster: a/(a−1) = 5/4 → 4a = 5a − 5 → a = 5 m/s. Time = 2000 / 5 = **400 s** (= 6 min 40 s).

practice.note: Return-to-START trap. To be back at the start each swimmer needs a whole ROUND trip (2 lengths), so use 2× the one-way times. LCM(30,40)=120 is the baited one-way answer — at 120 s they're at opposite walls, not together.
practice.solution: Round-trip times: Alice 2·30 = 60 s, Bob 2·40 = 80 s. Next simultaneous return to start = LCM(60,80). 60 = 2²·3·5, 80 = 2⁴·5 → LCM = 2⁴·3·5 = **240 s**.

practice.note: Average-speed trap. Weight by TIME via total distance / total time; averaging 1 and 0.5 to get 0.75 is wrong. Keep D symbolic — it cancels.
Percent-stacking. 'Both coupons simultaneously' means multiply the remaining-fractions; do NOT add 10%+20% = 30%. Order doesn't matter — multiplication commutes.

why: On the placement you nailed the geometric partial-sum question (2025-r8-t4) but by guessing, and you blew 2023-r1-b19 by head-adding 1+3+9+27+81 as "11" when it is 121 — same root gap both times: you can spot a geometric sequence but don't yet own the closed-form sums, so you fall back to shaky mental addition and either miss or get lucky.
overview: Bank sequence problems cluster into four shapes: (1) **arithmetic-vs-geometric sum comparisons** ("both start 1 and 3, find the difference of the sums"), (2) **geometric partial/infinite sums** — bouncing balls, "sum of first n = X, find n", (3) **recursive/Fibonacci** problems where you back-solve an early term, and (4) **careful-summation** integer puzzles (1..100, doubling). The mindset: in the first second, classify — constant *difference* = arithmetic, constant *ratio* = geometric — then reach for the closed form instead of adding a list. Geometric sums grow violently (ratio 3 over 5 terms already hits 121), so any "small" mental total is a red flag; write the closed form and evaluate. Own three formulas cold — arithmetic sum, finite geometric sum, infinite geometric sum — plus the powers-of-2 and 1..n anchors, and 80% of these become 5-second buzzes.

cards.title: Arithmetic sum: S = n·(a₁+aₙ)/2
cards.body: Sum = (number of terms) × (average of first and last). **Why:** pair terms outside-in — first+last, second+second-to-last — every pair sums to a₁+aₙ, and there are n/2 pairs, so S = (n/2)(a₁+aₙ). Gauss's trick. Equivalently an arithmetic list is symmetric, so its mean is (a₁+aₙ)/2 and sum = mean×count — **"sum = average × count" is your single most useful mental tool here.** Ex: 1,3,5,7,9 → 5·(1+9)/2 = 25.

cards.title: Number of terms: n = (aₙ−a₁)/d + 1
cards.body: Steps of size d from a₁ to aₙ, then **+1** for the starting term. **Why:** (aₙ−a₁)/d is the number of *gaps*; fence posts are always one more than gaps. This is the #1 off-by-one trap in the bank — the +1 is almost always what they're testing. Ex: 2,7,12,…,47 with d=5 → (47−2)/5+1 = 10 terms.

cards.title: Where the geometric sum comes from (multiply-and-subtract)
cards.body: Don't memorize a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r) blindly — you can rebuild it in 10 seconds. Write S = a+ar+ar²+…+arⁿ⁻¹. Multiply by r: rS = ar+ar²+…+arⁿ. Subtract: S−rS = a−arⁿ (every middle term cancels). So S(1−r)=a(1−rⁿ) ⇒ **S = a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)**. The telescoping cancellation is the whole trick; if you blank mid-round, reconstruct it this way.

cards.title: Finite geometric sum: S = a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)
cards.body: a = first term, r = ratio (any term ÷ previous), n = number of terms. **Why:** multiply-and-subtract card above — the middle telescopes. **Speed tip:** if the terms are positive and r>1, use the equivalent a(rⁿ−1)/(r−1) to avoid fractions. Ex: 1+3+9+27+81 = 1·(3⁵−1)/(3−1) = 242/2 = 121.

cards.title: Where the infinite geometric sum comes from (self-similarity)
cards.body: For |r|<1: S = a+ar+ar²+… Everything after the first term is r times the *whole* sum again, so S = a + r·S. Solve: S(1−r)=a ⇒ **S = a/(1−r)**. The tail of a geometric series is just a shrunk copy of itself — cleanest one-line derivation (also the rⁿ→0 limit of the finite form). Ex: 1+½+¼+… = 1/(1−½) = 2.

cards.title: Partial sum = total − tail (the fast way to "find n")
cards.body: For |r|<1, the sum of the first n terms is the infinite total *minus everything past term n*: **Sₙ = a/(1−r) − (tail)**, where tail = a·rⁿ/(1−r). Because the tail is one clean power, "sum of first n = X, find n" problems collapse to matching a single power of r. This is faster than expanding a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r) and solving — see the 2025-r8-t4 practice.

cards.title: Powers of 2: 1+2+4+…+2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1
cards.body: Sum up to 2ᵏ is one below the next power. **Why:** each running total sits one under the next term (1, 3=4−1, 7=8−1, 15…); in binary it's (k+1) ones, and adding 1 rolls over to a single 1 then zeros. This is the engine of 'each term = sum of all previous' problems: after the seed, every term equals the running total, so the list **doubles** (1,1,2,4,8,16,32,64).

cards.title: First n integers: 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2
cards.body: **Why:** it's the arithmetic sum with a₁=1, aₙ=n: n(1+n)/2. Pairs 1+n, 2+(n−1),… each = n+1, and there are n/2 pairs. **Anchor 1..100 = 5050 cold.** Used in 2025-r6-b1: true sum 5050, glitched sum 5599, excess = 549 = 9n ⇒ n=61 (appending a 0 turns n into 10n, an excess of exactly 9n).

cards.title: Symmetric-terms trick (2024-r5-b7)
cards.body: 'Three-term arithmetic, common difference 3, sum of squares = 381, find first term.' Don't set first = a and expand (a)²+(a+3)²+(a+6)². **Center on the middle term m:** terms are m−3, m, m+3, so sum of squares = 3m²+18 (cross terms ±6m cancel!). 3m²+18=381 ⇒ m²=121 ⇒ m=±11. First term = m−3 = 8 (positive root; m=−11 gives first term −14, so read which sign the bank wants). Centering on the middle kills the linear terms in **any** symmetric arithmetic sum-of-powers problem.

cards.title: Classify in one second: difference vs ratio vs self-referential
cards.body: 'arithmetic', 'common difference', 'increasing by' → S=n(a₁+aₙ)/2. 'geometric', 'common ratio', 'each term is __× the previous', '20% less each time', 'bounces', 'fractal', 'infinitely many', 'as time → ∞' → geometric sum (a/(1−r) if infinite; **check for a one-time initial piece** like the first drop). 'each term is the sum of the previous two' → Fibonacci recurrence, back-solve algebraically. 'sum of first n = X, find n' → set closed form (or total−tail) equal and match a power. 'each term = sum of ALL previous' → it doubles after the seed.

cards.title: Your 2023-r1-b19 miss: geometric sums explode — never head-add them

(2) Use the closed form: 1·(3⁵−1)/(3−1) = 242/2 = 121; arithmetic 1,3,5,7,9 = 25; difference 96. With the formula the '11' error is structurally impossible. Sister traps: the bounce problem (count both **down and up**, total = drop + 2·Σheights) and the +1 off-by-one when counting terms.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT MISS (you got 11, answer is 96). Both sequences start 1, 3 — that pins d=2 for the arithmetic and r=3 for the geometric. The whole question is 'can you sum a 5-term geometric series without mis-adding.'
practice.solution: Arithmetic (a₁=1, d=2): 1,3,5,7,9 → 5·(1+9)/2 = 25. Geometric (a=1, r=3): 1,3,9,27,81 → (3⁵−1)/(3−1) = 242/2 = 121. Positive difference = 121 − 25 = **96**. Using the closed form instead of head-adding makes the '11' error impossible.

practice.note: YOUR PLACEMENT GUESS (right but lucky). Canonical 'sum of first n = X, find n.' Own the total-minus-tail path so it's a 5-second buzz.
practice.solution: First three terms ¼, ⅛, 1/16 ⇒ a=¼, r=½. Infinite total = a/(1−r) = ¼/½ = ½ = 64/128. Fast path: Sₙ = total − tail, so tail = 64/128 − 63/128 = 1/128 = (½)⁷. Tail = a·rⁿ/(1−r) = (½)·(½)ⁿ = (½)ⁿ⁺¹, so n+1 = 7 ⇒ **n = 6**. (Algebra check: ½(1−(½)ⁿ)=63/128 ⇒ (½)ⁿ=1/64 ⇒ n=6.)

practice.note: Infinite geometric with the classic distractor: the ball travels DOWN then UP on every bounce, but the very first drop happens only once. Missing the ×2, or double-counting the drop, is the trap.
practice.solution: Drop = 5 ft (once). '20% less' ⇒ r = 0.8; first bounce peak = 0.8·5 = 4 ft, and each bounce height is traveled twice (up+down). Bounce distance = 2·(4 + 4·0.8 + …) = 2·[4/(1−0.8)] = 2·20 = 40. Total = 5 + 40 = **45 ft**.

practice.note: 'Each term is the sum of ALL previous terms' — recognize this doubles after the seed; don't re-add every time. Tests careful summation, your weak spot.
practice.solution: a₁=1. a₂ = sum of previous = 1. From then on each term equals the running total, which equals the previous term again, so it doubles: 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. The 8th term = **64**. Shortcut: for k≥2, aₖ = 2ᵏ⁻² (a₂=2⁰,…,a₈=2⁶=64).

practice.note: Three-term arithmetic, common difference 3, sum of squares 381 → first term. Center on the MIDDLE term so cross terms cancel; two roots exist, the bank wants the positive-first one.
practice.solution: Let the terms be m−3, m, m+3. Sum of squares = (m−3)²+m²+(m+3)² = 3m² + 18 = 381 ⇒ m² = 121 ⇒ m = 11 (positive root ⇒ sequence 8,11,14). First term = 11 − 3 = **8**.

practice.note: Fibonacci-style recurrence (each term = sum of previous two), a₂ and a₆ given → back-solve for a₁. Carry one unknown forward; don't guess-and-check.
practice.solution: Let a₁=x, a₂=5. Then a₃=x+5, a₄=x+10, a₅=2x+15, a₆=a₄+a₅=3x+25. Set 3x+25 = 1 ⇒ x = **−8** (sequence −8,5,−3,2,−1,1 ✓). Speed shortcut: coefficients are Fibonacci — a₆ = F₄·a₁ + F₅·a₂ = 3a₁ + 5a₂ = 3x+25, same equation instantly.
